key_terms.meaning: P<sub>t</sub> = P<sub>c</sub>(1 + m²/2); η = m²/(2 + m²), at most 33.3 %
s(t) = A<sub>c</sub> m(t) cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t; bandwidth 2W; no carrier line
y(t) = (A<sub>c</sub>/2) m(t) cos φ; zero at φ = 90°
m(t) cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t ∓ m̂(t) sin 2πf<sub>c</sub>t; bandwidth W
B = W + f<sub>v</sub>; filter condition H(f<sub>c</sub> + x) + H(f<sub>c</sub> − x) = 1
i = a<sub>0</sub> + a<sub>1</sub>v + a<sub>2</sub>v²; m = 2a<sub>2</sub>A<sub>m</sub>/a<sub>1</sub>; needs f<sub>c</sub> > 3W
f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>s</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub>; image f<sub>si</sub> = f<sub>s</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub> (high-side)
B<sub>T</sub> = N·B<sub>ch</sub> + (N − 1)·B<sub>g</sub>; basic group 12 × 4 kHz in 60 to 108 kHz

takeaways: AM puts the message on the envelope: three lines, a carrier and two sidebands of mA<sub>c</sub>/2, in a band of 2f<sub>m</sub> whatever m is.
Power splits as P<sub>c</sub>(1 + m²/2); at most a third of it, at m = 1, carries the message. Several tones add as m<sub>t</sub>² = m<sub>1</sub>² + m<sub>2</sub>².
DSB-SC drops the carrier and needs a locked local carrier: a phase error scales the output by cos φ, a frequency error makes it beat.
SSB sends one sideband in a band of W; a frequency error shifts its tones. VSB adds a vestige so a real filter can handle video.
A square law multiplies: one device and a filter give AM, two in balance give DSB-SC with the carrier cancelled.
The envelope detector's RC must bridge carrier periods but follow the fastest envelope fall; the AC load limits m to R<sub>ac</sub>/R<sub>dc</sub>.
High-level modulation keeps class C efficiency but needs an audio modulator of P<sub>dc</sub> m²/2; low-level needs linear stages.
A superhet does its gain and selectivity at a fixed IF; the image at f<sub>s</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub> must be rejected before the mixer.
FDM stacks SSB channels in slots with guard bands; total band = channels plus guard bands, and guard bands do not double with DSB.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the AM power derivation with a numerical problem, the balanced modulator and envelope detector circuits, SSB generation by the filter and phase-shift methods, and the superheterodyne receiver with image frequency; FDM usually appears as a block diagram with a bandwidth calculation.

bank.q: Derive the expression for a tone-modulated AM wave, sketch its waveform and spectrum, and show that the total power is P<sub>c</sub>(1 + m²/2). Find the maximum transmission efficiency, and show how m is measured from V<sub>max</sub> and V<sub>min</sub>.
outline: Carrier and message; s(t) = A<sub>c</sub>[1 + m cos 2πf<sub>m</sub>t] cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t with m = A<sub>m</sub>/A<sub>c</sub>
Expansion into carrier, USB and LSB; amplitudes mA<sub>c</sub>/2; bandwidth 2f<sub>m</sub>
Power of each line, P<sub>t</sub> = P<sub>c</sub>(1 + m²/2), η = m²/(2 + m²), 33.3 % at m = 1
V<sub>max</sub> = A<sub>c</sub>(1 + m), V<sub>min</sub> = A<sub>c</sub>(1 − m), m = (V<sub>max</sub> − V<sub>min</sub>)/(V<sub>max</sub> + V<sub>min</sub>)
answer: Let the carrier be A<sub>c</sub> cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t and the message a tone A<sub>m</sub> cos 2πf<sub>m</sub>t with f<sub>m</sub> ≪ f<sub>c</sub>. In conventional AM the carrier amplitude follows the message: the instantaneous amplitude is A<sub>c</sub> + A<sub>m</sub> cos 2πf<sub>m</sub>t.

answer.text: Write the wave and take A<sub>c</sub> out of the bracket:
answer.pre:
s(t) = [A<sub>c</sub> + A<sub>m</sub> cos 2πf<sub>m</sub>t] cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t
     = A<sub>c</sub>[1 + m cos 2πf<sub>m</sub>t] cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t,   m = A<sub>m</sub>/A<sub>c</sub>

answer: The bracket A<sub>c</sub>[1 + m cos 2πf<sub>m</sub>t] is the envelope. For m ≤ 1 it never goes negative, so the outline of the wave has exactly the shape of the message. The waveform sketch is a carrier whose peaks follow this envelope (Figure 2.1.1, top). For m > 1 the bracket changes sign, the carrier phase reverses and the envelope is distorted: overmodulation.

answer.text: Expand the product with 2 cos A cos B = cos(A − B) + cos(A + B):
answer.pre:
s(t) = A<sub>c</sub> cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t
     + (mA<sub>c</sub>/2) cos 2π(f<sub>c</sub> + f<sub>m</sub>)t      (upper sideband)
     + (mA<sub>c</sub>/2) cos 2π(f<sub>c</sub> − f<sub>m</sub>)t      (lower sideband)

answer: The spectrum has three lines: the carrier of height A<sub>c</sub> at f<sub>c</sub> and two sidebands of height mA<sub>c</sub>/2 at f<sub>c</sub> ± f<sub>m</sub> (Figure 2.1.1, bottom). The band runs from f<sub>c</sub> − f<sub>m</sub> to f<sub>c</sub> + f<sub>m</sub>, so B = 2f<sub>m</sub>, whatever the value of m.

answer.text: Power: a cosine of peak V across R gives V²/(2R). Line by line:
answer.pre:
P<sub>c</sub>   = A<sub>c</sub>²/(2R)
P<sub>USB</sub> = (mA<sub>c</sub>/2)²/(2R) = m²A<sub>c</sub>²/(8R) = m²P<sub>c</sub>/4
P<sub>LSB</sub> = m²P<sub>c</sub>/4
P<sub>t</sub>   = P<sub>c</sub> + m²P<sub>c</sub>/4 + m²P<sub>c</sub>/4 = P<sub>c</sub>(1 + m²/2)

answer: The efficiency is the sideband share of the power: η = (m²P<sub>c</sub>/2)/[P<sub>c</sub>(1 + m²/2)] = m²/(2 + m²). It rises with m, and the largest m that avoids overmodulation is 1, so η<sub>max</sub> = 1/3 = 33.3 %. Two thirds of the power, at best, goes into the carrier, which carries no message.

Measuring m: the envelope peaks at V<sub>max</sub> = A<sub>c</sub>(1 + m) and dips to V<sub>min</sub> = A<sub>c</sub>(1 − m). Then V<sub>max</sub> − V<sub>min</sub> = 2mA<sub>c</sub> and V<sub>max</sub> + V<sub>min</sub> = 2A<sub>c</sub>, so m = (V<sub>max</sub> − V<sub>min</sub>)/(V<sub>max</sub> + V<sub>min</sub>). Half the sum gives A<sub>c</sub> and half the difference gives A<sub>m</sub>.

answer.text: Numerical check with A<sub>c</sub> = 10 V, m = 0.6 and R = 50 Ω:

answer: Check: P<sub>c</sub> + 2 × 0.09 = 1.18 W, the same as P<sub>c</sub>(1 + m²/2) = 1.18 W; and the sideband share 0.18/1.18 = 15.3 % matches m²/(2 + m²).

bank.q: Explain how a balanced modulator produces DSB-SC, deriving its output for square-law devices. Then explain coherent detection of DSB-SC and the effect of phase and frequency errors in the local carrier, and how a Costas loop removes them.
outline: Square-law model i = a<sub>0</sub> + a<sub>1</sub>v + a<sub>2</sub>v²
v<sub>1</sub> = c + m, v<sub>2</sub> = c − m; i<sub>1</sub> − i<sub>2</sub> = 2a<sub>1</sub>m + 4a<sub>2</sub>cm; carrier cancels
Coherent detector: multiply by cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + φ), LPF, y = (A<sub>c</sub>/2)m(t) cos φ
Phase error: cos φ loss, null at 90°; frequency error: beat cos 2πΔft
Costas loop: I and Q arms, error ∝ m² sin 2φ
answer: A balanced modulator uses two matched nonlinear devices (diodes or transistors) whose current, for small inputs, is i = a<sub>0</sub> + a<sub>1</sub>v + a<sub>2</sub>v². The carrier c(t) = A<sub>c</sub> cos ω<sub>c</sub>t is fed to both in the same phase and the message m(t) in opposite phase, through a centre-tapped input transformer: v<sub>1</sub> = c + m and v<sub>2</sub> = c − m. A centre-tapped output transformer delivers the difference of the two currents.

answer.text: Difference of the currents:
answer.pre:
i<sub>1</sub> = a<sub>0</sub> + a<sub>1</sub>(c + m) + a<sub>2</sub>(c + m)²
i<sub>2</sub> = a<sub>0</sub> + a<sub>1</sub>(c − m) + a<sub>2</sub>(c − m)²
i<sub>1</sub> − i<sub>2</sub> = 2a<sub>1</sub>m + a<sub>2</sub>[(c + m)² − (c − m)²]
          = 2a<sub>1</sub>m(t) + 4a<sub>2</sub>c(t)m(t)

answer: The terms a<sub>0</sub>, a<sub>1</sub>c, a<sub>2</sub>c² and a<sub>2</sub>m² are the same in both currents and cancel; in particular the carrier a<sub>1</sub>c vanishes. The term 4a<sub>2</sub>c(t)m(t) is the product we want. A band-pass filter centred on f<sub>c</sub> with bandwidth 2W removes the low-frequency term 2a<sub>1</sub>m(t). The output, 4a<sub>2</sub>A<sub>c</sub> m(t) cos ω<sub>c</sub>t, is DSB-SC.

answer.text: Numbers: with a<sub>1</sub> = 10 mA/V, a<sub>2</sub> = 2 mA/V², A<sub>c</sub> = 2 V and a 0.5 V tone at 1 kHz on a 100 kHz carrier:

answer: Coherent detection: the receiver multiplies the DSB-SC wave s(t) = A<sub>c</sub> m(t) cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t by a local carrier cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + φ) and low-pass filters the product.

answer.text: Using cos A cos B = ½[cos(A − B) + cos(A + B)]:
answer.pre:
s(t) cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + φ) = (A<sub>c</sub>/2) m(t) cos φ + (A<sub>c</sub>/2) m(t) cos(4πf<sub>c</sub>t + φ)
LPF output: y(t) = (A<sub>c</sub>/2) m(t) cos φ

answer: Phase error: the output is scaled by cos φ. For the tone above, the 4 mA sidebands demodulate (with a unit-gain multiplier) to 4.00 mA·cos φ: 4.00 at φ = 0, 2.83 at 45° and 0 at 90°, the quadrature null effect. A slowly drifting φ makes the sound fade in and out.

Frequency error: with a local carrier at f<sub>c</sub> + Δf the output is (A<sub>c</sub>/2) m(t) cos 2πΔft. The message is multiplied by a slow beat, so a 1 kHz tone with Δf = 5 Hz comes out as 995 Hz and 1005 Hz together: a tone that swells and fades five times a second.

Costas loop: a voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) drives two multipliers, one directly (I arm) and one through a 90° shift (Q arm). After low-pass filters the arms give (A<sub>c</sub>/2)m(t) cos φ and (A<sub>c</sub>/2)m(t) sin φ. A third multiplier forms their product (A<sub>c</sub>²/8)m²(t) sin 2φ, which, after a narrow loop filter, steers the VCO. Since m²(t) ≥ 0, the sign of the control voltage is the sign of φ near lock, and it is zero at φ = 0. The loop therefore holds the VCO on the incoming carrier's frequency and phase, and the I arm is the demodulated output.

Closing check: with φ = 0 the loop control voltage (A<sub>c</sub>²/8)m² sin 0 = 0 and the I arm holds the full message; with φ = 90° the I arm is zero and the Q arm is full, so a loop that locked there would be visibly wrong, which is why the sign of the control drives it back to φ = 0.

bank.q: Explain the filter and phase-shift methods of generating SSB, proving with a tone that the phase-shift method gives one sideband. Explain VSB and the condition its filter must meet, and state where each is used.
outline: SSB keeps one sideband; B = W; power saving
Filter method: DSB-SC then band-pass; needs a gap below 300 Hz; low carrier then mix up
Phase-shift method: m cos ω<sub>c</sub>t ∓ m̂ sin ω<sub>c</sub>t; Hilbert transform; tone proof
VSB: one sideband plus vestige f<sub>v</sub>; B = W + f<sub>v</sub>
Condition H(f<sub>c</sub> + x) + H(f<sub>c</sub> − x) = 1; TV video use
answer: SSB sends only one sideband of a DSB-SC signal. The two sidebands are mirror images and each holds the whole message, so the bandwidth falls from 2W to W and, for a test tone at m = 1, the radiated power falls from 1.5P<sub>c</sub> for AM to 0.25P<sub>c</sub>.

Filter method: a balanced modulator makes DSB-SC and a band-pass filter keeps one sideband. Speech carries almost nothing below 300 Hz, so around the carrier there is a gap of 2 × 300 = 600 Hz between the inner edges of the two sidebands. The filter must pass fully on one side of this gap and reject strongly on the other. At 100 kHz this is a 0.6 % transition, which crystal or mechanical filters can achieve; at tens of megahertz it is not, so the SSB signal is made at a low carrier and then mixed up to the final frequency.

Phase-shift (Hartley) method: two balanced modulators are used. The first multiplies m(t) by cos ω<sub>c</sub>t. The second multiplies m̂(t), the Hilbert transform of m(t) (every positive-frequency component delayed by 90°), by sin ω<sub>c</sub>t, the carrier shifted by 90°. The outputs are subtracted for the USB or added for the LSB.

answer.text: Proof with a tone m(t) = cos ω<sub>m</sub>t, for which m̂(t) = sin ω<sub>m</sub>t:
answer.pre:
s<sub>USB</sub> = cos ω<sub>m</sub>t cos ω<sub>c</sub>t − sin ω<sub>m</sub>t sin ω<sub>c</sub>t = cos(ω<sub>c</sub> + ω<sub>m</sub>)t
s<sub>LSB</sub> = cos ω<sub>m</sub>t cos ω<sub>c</sub>t + sin ω<sub>m</sub>t sin ω<sub>c</sub>t = cos(ω<sub>c</sub> − ω<sub>m</sub>)t

answer: Only one line remains in each case. For f<sub>c</sub> = 100 kHz and f<sub>m</sub> = 1 kHz the USB output is a single line at 101 kHz. No sharp filter is needed, but the 90° shift must be accurate over the whole audio band and the two branches must match; a phase error leaves part of the unwanted sideband. The Weaver method avoids the wideband phase shifter by first mixing with an audio tone at the band centre, low-pass filtering, then mixing with the carrier in two quadrature branches.

VSB keeps one sideband in full, a vestige of width f<sub>v</sub> of the other, and lets the filter roll off gradually through f<sub>c</sub>. Its bandwidth is W + f<sub>v</sub>. It is used where the message has energy down to almost 0 Hz, such as television video, so that no gap exists for an SSB filter. In the PAL-B system once used for Indian terrestrial TV the video band is 5 MHz and the vestige 0.75 MHz, giving 5.75 MHz of video in a 7 MHz channel.

answer.text: After coherent detection the vestige folds onto the upper sideband near f<sub>c</sub>. The message is undistorted only if, for |x| ≤ f<sub>v</sub>,
answer.pre: H(f<sub>c</sub> + x) + H(f<sub>c</sub> − x) = 1

answer.text: Check with a straight-line filter rising from 0 at f<sub>c</sub> − 0.75 MHz to 1 at f<sub>c</sub> + 0.75 MHz, H = 0.5 + x/1.5:

answer: Uses: SSB for HF voice links, marine and amateur radio and the old FDM telephone trunks; VSB for analog TV video and, in digital form (8-VSB), for one digital TV standard. Closing check: for 0.3 to 3.4 kHz speech on 100 kHz, DSB occupies 6.8 kHz, SSB 3.4 kHz and VSB with a 0.5 kHz vestige 3.9 kHz, so VSB costs 0.5 kHz more than SSB and saves 2.9 kHz against DSB.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of a superheterodyne AM receiver and explain each stage. Explain the image frequency, image-rejection ratio, tracking and the choice of intermediate frequency.
outline: Blocks: RF stage, mixer, LO, IF amplifier, detector, AGC, audio
Image f<sub>si</sub> = f<sub>s</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub>; must be rejected before the mixer; α = √(1 + Q²ρ²)
Tracking: ganged capacitor, padder, three-point tracking
Choice of IF: image rejection vs selectivity; not in the band
answer: Block diagram, in signal order: antenna → RF stage (tuned amplifier) → mixer ← local oscillator (LO) → IF amplifier (fixed, 455 kHz) → envelope detector → audio amplifier → loudspeaker, with an AGC line from the detector back to the RF and IF stages (Figure 2.7.1).

RF stage: a tuned circuit, ganged with the LO, selects the wanted station f<sub>s</sub>, provides the image rejection and, with an amplifier, improves sensitivity and noise figure. Mixer and LO: the mixer multiplies the RF by f<sub>LO</sub>; its output tank keeps the difference f<sub>LO</sub> − f<sub>s</sub> = f<sub>IF</sub>. IF amplifier: two or three fixed tuned stages or a ceramic filter give most of the gain and set selectivity (about 10 kHz bandwidth for AM broadcast). Detector: an envelope detector recovers the audio and a DC level proportional to the carrier. AGC: the DC level, filtered, reduces RF and IF gain on strong stations so that output stays nearly constant. Audio amplifier: drives the speaker.

Why a superhet: amplifiers and filters at one fixed frequency can be made with high gain, steep skirts and a flat top once and for all; stages that must tune across 540 to 1650 kHz cannot. Changing the station only moves the LO and the RF tuning.

answer.text: Image: with high-side injection,
answer.pre:
f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>s</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub>
f<sub>si</sub> = f<sub>s</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub>   (image)
f<sub>si</sub> − f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>IF</sub>

answer: The image is a second input frequency, f<sub>IF</sub> above the LO, that the mixer also turns into f<sub>IF</sub>. Once both are at 455 kHz no IF filter can separate them, so the rejection must happen before the mixer, in the tuned RF stages.

answer.text: Image-rejection ratio of one tuned circuit of quality factor Q:
answer.pre: ρ = f<sub>si</sub>/f<sub>s</sub> − f<sub>s</sub>/f<sub>si</sub>,   α = √(1 + Q²ρ²)

answer.text: Numbers for f<sub>IF</sub> = 455 kHz and Q = 60:

answer: Rejection is worse at the top of the band, because the image is a smaller fraction away. Two tuned stages multiply: at 1650 kHz, 54.4² = 2 962, or 69.4 dB.

Tracking: one knob turns a ganged capacitor that tunes the RF circuit and the LO together, keeping f<sub>LO</sub> − f<sub>s</sub> = 455 kHz. The RF section spans 540 to 1650 kHz, a ratio of 3.06 (capacitance ratio 9.34); the LO spans 995 to 2105 kHz, a ratio of 2.12 (capacitance ratio 4.48). A series padder and a parallel trimmer reduce the LO section's range, and the error is made zero at three points of the band (three-point tracking).

Choice of IF: a high IF puts the image far away (better image rejection) and eases tracking; a low IF gives narrower, steeper IF filters (better adjacent-channel selectivity) and more stable gain. The IF must lie outside the tuning band. 455 kHz is the usual compromise for medium wave; shortwave sets use a higher first IF or double conversion.
Closing check: at 540 kHz, f<sub>LO</sub> = 995 kHz and f<sub>si</sub> = 1450 kHz; 1450 − 995 = 455 kHz, the same IF as 995 − 540, which confirms the image.

bank.q: Explain the working of a diode envelope detector and state the conditions on its time constant. What are diagonal clipping and negative-peak clipping?
outline: Charge on peaks, discharge through R
answer: Circuit: the AM wave feeds a diode in series with a load resistor R shunted by a capacitor C; a coupling capacitor C<sub>c</sub> takes the audio to the next stage, whose input resistance is R<sub>i</sub> (Figure 2.5.1).

Working: on each positive carrier peak the diode conducts and charges C nearly to the peak through the small source and diode resistance. Between peaks the diode is reverse biased and C discharges slowly through R. The capacitor voltage therefore follows the envelope A<sub>c</sub>[1 + m cos 2πf<sub>m</sub>t] with a small sawtooth ripple at f<sub>c</sub>. C<sub>c</sub> removes the DC part A<sub>c</sub> and passes the audio A<sub>c</sub>m cos 2πf<sub>m</sub>t; the DC part is used for AGC.
Lower limit (ripple): between peaks C falls by about 1/(f<sub>c</sub>RC) of its voltage, so RC ≫ 1/f<sub>c</sub>.

Upper limit (diagonal clipping): if RC is too long, C cannot discharge as fast as the envelope falls and the output slides down an exponential instead of following the envelope. For a tone the output follows the envelope everywhere only if RC ≤ √(1 − m²)/(2πf<sub>m</sub>m).

Negative-peak clipping: for audio the load is R<sub>ac</sub> = R ∥ R<sub>i</sub>, smaller than R<sub>dc</sub> = R. The audio swing on R<sub>ac</sub> cannot exceed what the DC level allows, so the troughs are cut flat unless m ≤ R<sub>ac</sub>/R<sub>dc</sub>.

answer.text: Numbers for a detector at the 455 kHz IF with W = 5 kHz, m = 0.8, R = 5 kΩ and R<sub>i</sub> = 20 kΩ:

answer: Closing check: RC = 20 µs lies between 2.20 µs and 23.9 µs, and m = 0.8 just equals R<sub>ac</sub>/R<sub>dc</sub> = 0.8, so this detector is at the edge of negative-peak clipping. The 10.4 % ripple at 455 kHz is removed by a small RC filter after the detector.

bank.q: A nonlinear device has i = 20v + 4v² mA (v in volts). It is driven by v = 1.5 cos(2π × 500 × 10³t) + 0.3 cos(2π × 4 × 10³t) V and loaded by a tank tuned to 500 kHz with a dynamic resistance of 500 Ω and bandwidth 8 kHz. Find every frequency in the device current with its amplitude, the AM output voltages and m, the message amplitude needed for m = 0.5, and the output of a balanced modulator built from two such devices.
outline: List DC, f<sub>m</sub>, 2f<sub>m</sub>, f<sub>c</sub> ± f<sub>m</sub>, f<sub>c</sub>, 2f<sub>c</sub> with amplitudes
Tank passes f<sub>c</sub> and f<sub>c</sub> ± f<sub>m</sub>
answer: Coefficients: a<sub>1</sub> = 20 mA/V, a<sub>2</sub> = 4 mA/V²; A<sub>c</sub> = 1.5 V at f<sub>c</sub> = 500 kHz; A<sub>m</sub> = 0.3 V at f<sub>m</sub> = 4 kHz.
The linear term a<sub>1</sub>v copies the inputs. The square term a<sub>2</sub>v² gives DC, second harmonics and the product, using cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2 and 2 cos A cos B = cos(A − B) + cos(A + B).

answer.text: Every component of the device current:

answer: The tank, centred on 500 kHz with 8 kHz bandwidth, passes 496 to 504 kHz and rejects DC, 4 kHz, 8 kHz and 1000 kHz. The condition f<sub>c</sub> > 3W, here 500 kHz > 12 kHz, is met easily, so the 8 kHz line is nowhere near the passband.

answer.text: Output voltages across 500 Ω and the modulation index:
answer.pre:
carrier  = 30.0 mA × 500 Ω = 15.0 V
sideband = 1.80 mA × 500 Ω = 0.90 V each
m = 2 × sideband/carrier = 2 × 1.80/30.0 = 0.12
check: 2a<sub>2</sub>A<sub>m</sub>/a<sub>1</sub> = 2 × 4 × 0.3/20 = 0.12

answer: For m = 0.5: A<sub>m</sub> = m·a<sub>1</sub>/(2a<sub>2</sub>) = 0.5 × 20/8 = 1.25 V. That is almost as large as the 1.5 V carrier, and at such a level the a<sub>3</sub>v³ term of a real device is no longer negligible; it adds lines at f<sub>c</sub> ± 2f<sub>m</sub> (492 and 508 kHz) that fall inside the passband. Square-law modulators are therefore run at small m.

answer.text: Balanced modulator: v<sub>1</sub>,2 = 1.5 cos ω<sub>c</sub>t ± 0.3 cos ω<sub>m</sub>t, output i<sub>1</sub> − i<sub>2</sub> = 2a<sub>1</sub>m(t) + 4a<sub>2</sub>c(t)m(t):

answer: The balanced output is DSB-SC with sidebands twice the single-device value (3.6 mA against 1.80 mA) and no carrier.
Closing check: carrier 15.0 V with sidebands of 0.90 V gives m = 2 × 0.90/15.0 = 0.12, the same as the formula.

bank.q: Design the envelope detector of an AM receiver that works at the 455 kHz IF. The highest audio frequency is 5 kHz, the deepest modulation is m = 0.8, the load resistor is 5 kΩ and the audio stage that follows has an input resistance of 20 kΩ. Choose C, find the ripple, check diagonal and negative-peak clipping, and say what happens on passages with m = 0.9.
answer: Data: f<sub>c</sub> = 455 kHz (the detector sits after the IF amplifier), W = 5 kHz, m = 0.8, R = 5 kΩ, R<sub>i</sub> = 20 kΩ.

answer.text: Step 1, lower limit from ripple:
Step 2, upper limit from diagonal clipping:

answer: The rough rule RC ≪ 1/(2πW) = 31.8 µs is looser than this exact limit at m = 0.8, so the exact limit governs.

answer.text: Step 3, trial values of RC and the resulting C and ripple:

answer: Choose RC = 20 µs, C = 4 nF: the longest value that keeps a margin below 23.9 µs, with 10.4 % ripple. Because the IF is only about 100 times the top audio frequency, the ripple cannot be made as small as at RF; a simple RC low-pass after the detector removes the 455 kHz residue, and the audio stage does not respond to it anyway.

answer.text: Step 4, negative-peak clipping:
answer.pre:
R<sub>ac</sub> = R ∥ R<sub>i</sub> = (5 × 20)/(5 + 20) = 4 kΩ
R<sub>ac</sub>/R<sub>dc</sub> = 4/5 = 0.8

answer: With m = 0.8 the requirement m ≤ R<sub>ac</sub>/R<sub>dc</sub> is met with no margin: the troughs just touch the clipping level. A larger R<sub>i</sub>, or splitting R into two parts and taking the audio from the tap, would add margin.

Step 5, passages at m = 0.9: the diagonal-clipping limit falls to √(1 − 0.81)/(2π × 5000 × 0.9) = 15.4 µs, below the chosen 20 µs, so 5 kHz tones at that depth are clipped diagonally; and 0.9 > 0.8, so the troughs are also clipped at the AC load. Both faults appear only on the loudest high-pitched passages.

answer.text: Design summary:

answer: Closing check: 2.20 µs ≪ 20 µs ≤ 23.9 µs, and C = 20 × 10⁻⁶/5000 = 4 × 10⁻⁹ F = 4 nF.

bank.q: A medium-wave superhet tunes 540 to 1650 kHz with a 455 kHz IF and high-side injection. Find the LO range and the capacitance ratios of the RF and LO sections. Find the image frequency and the image-rejection ratio at both band edges for one tuned RF circuit with Q = 60, and for two such circuits. Then find the rejection for a 20 MHz shortwave signal with a 455 kHz IF and with a 10.7 MHz first IF, and comment.
outline: f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>s</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub>; ratios and capacitance ratios (square)
ρ = f<sub>si</sub>/f<sub>s</sub> − f<sub>s</sub>/f<sub>si</sub>; α = √(1 + Q²ρ²); dB

answer.text: LO range, high-side injection f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>s</sub> + 455 kHz:
answer.pre:
f<sub>LO</sub>(min) = 540 + 455 = 995 kHz
f<sub>LO</sub>(max) = 1650 + 455 = 2105 kHz

answer.text: Tuning ratios. A tuned circuit's frequency goes as 1/√C, so the capacitance ratio is the square of the frequency ratio:

answer: The LO section needs less than half the capacitance swing of the RF section, so on a ganged capacitor with identical sections the LO gets a series padder (reducing the maximum) and a parallel trimmer (raising the minimum). The tracking error is then zero at three points of the band and small between them. With low-side injection the LO would have to run from 85 to 1195 kHz, a frequency ratio of 14.1 and a capacitance ratio near 198, which no practical variable capacitor gives; this is the main reason broadcast receivers put the LO above the signal.

answer.text: Image frequencies: f<sub>si</sub> = f<sub>s</sub> + 2 × 455 = f<sub>s</sub> + 910 kHz.
answer.pre:
at 540 kHz:  f<sub>si</sub> = 1450 kHz
at 1650 kHz: f<sub>si</sub> = 2560 kHz

answer.text: Image rejection with ρ = f<sub>si</sub>/f<sub>s</sub> − f<sub>s</sub>/f<sub>si</sub> and α = √(1 + Q²ρ²), Q = 60:

answer: The rejection falls towards the top of the band because the fixed 910 kHz separation is a smaller fraction of a higher signal frequency. A receiver with only one tuned circuit before the mixer is weakest at 1650 kHz; a second tuned stage (an RF amplifier) squares the ratio.

answer.text: Shortwave signal at 20 MHz, Q = 60:

answer: Why the shortwave case is so much worse: ρ depends on the ratio f<sub>si</sub>/f<sub>s</sub>, not on the difference. At 540 kHz the image is 2.69 times the signal frequency; at 20 MHz with a 455 kHz IF it is only 1.0455 times, so the RF tuned circuit, whose bandwidth is f<sub>s</sub>/Q = 333 kHz at 20 MHz, hardly separates the two.

Comment: with a 455 kHz IF the image at 20.91 MHz is only 4.5 % above the signal, and one tuned circuit passes it only 5.43 times weaker (14.7 dB): stations would be heard on top of each other. A 10.7 MHz first IF puts the image at 41.4 MHz and gives 39.6 dB. Selectivity is then obtained with a second conversion to 455 kHz (double conversion), getting both good image rejection and narrow filters.

Closing check: at 1650 kHz, f<sub>si</sub> − f<sub>LO</sub> = 2560 − 2105 = 455 kHz, equal to f<sub>LO</sub> − f<sub>s</sub> = 2105 − 1650, so 2560 kHz is the image; and 20 log(54.4²) = 69.4 dB, twice the single-circuit 34.7 dB.

bank.q: Twenty-four telephone channels of 0.3 to 3.4 kHz are to be frequency multiplexed for a cable link. (a) Using SSB (lower sideband) in 4 kHz slots with the first carrier at 64 kHz, give the band of the lowest and highest channels, the guard band and the composite band. (b) Find the composite bandwidth if DSB-SC were used with 1 kHz guard bands between channels. (c) For a single test tone, compare the power one channel needs with SSB and with AM at m = 1 for the same carrier level.
outline: Carriers 64, 68, … kHz; LSB from f<sub>ci</sub> − 3.4 to f<sub>ci</sub> − 0.3
answer: Each voice channel is limited to 0.3 to 3.4 kHz, multiplied by its own carrier in a balanced modulator, and the lower sideband is kept by a crystal filter. Carriers are 4 kHz apart: 64, 68, 72, …, so channel k uses f<sub>ck</sub> = 64 + 4(k − 1) kHz.

answer.text: (a) Channel bands. The LSB of carrier f<sub>c</sub> runs from f<sub>c</sub> − 3.4 to f<sub>c</sub> − 0.3 kHz:

answer: Guard band between neighbours: 64.6 − 63.7 = 0.9 kHz (slot 4 kHz minus 3.1 kHz of speech, with 0.3 kHz below and 0.6 kHz above each band inside its slot). Composite band: 60 to 156 kHz, that is 24 × 4 = 96 kHz.

answer.text: (b) DSB-SC: each channel needs 2W = 6.8 kHz, with 23 guard bands of 1 kHz:

answer: So DSB-SC needs 186.2 kHz against 96 kHz for SSB, 1.94 times as much. The ratio is less than 2 because guard bands do not double.

answer.text: (c) Power per channel for one test tone, carrier level P<sub>c</sub>:

answer: AM would need 1.5/0.25 = 6 times the SSB power per channel, and on a cable with 24 channels the line amplifiers would have to carry all 24 carriers as well. Carriers would also create strong intermodulation products in the amplifiers. This is why telephone FDM used suppressed-carrier SSB.

Transmitter, channel by channel: low-pass filter to 3.4 kHz, balanced modulator with carrier f<sub>ck</sub>, crystal band-pass filter keeping f<sub>ck</sub> − 3.4 to f<sub>ck</sub> − 0.3 kHz, then a linear summer for all 24 channels. The summer and line amplifiers must be linear, because a nonlinearity would create intermodulation products, such as 2f<sub>1</sub> − f<sub>2</sub>, that fall inside other channels' slots as crosstalk.

Receiver: a bank of 24 band-pass filters separates the slots; each slot is coherently detected with its own carrier (all derived from one master oscillator so that an SSB frequency error does not shift the voice) and low-pass filtered to 3.4 kHz.
Closing check: channel 24's carrier is 64 + 4 × 23 = 156 kHz and its band ends at 155.7 kHz, inside the top slot that ends at 156 kHz; 24 slots × 4 kHz = 96 kHz = 156 − 60.

bank.q: Compare AM, DSB-SC, SSB and VSB for a message of bandwidth W in bandwidth, power, transmitter and receiver complexity, using a 10 kW carrier with a test tone at m = 1 and at m = 0.3. Recommend a scheme for medium-wave broadcasting, for HF point-to-point voice and for television video, giving reasons.
outline: Powers from P<sub>c</sub>(1 + m²/2), P<sub>c</sub>m²/2, P<sub>c</sub>m²/4
Transmitter: high-level for AM; low-level linear for SSB/VSB
answer: All four schemes are linear: the modulated wave is a shifted copy of the message spectrum. They differ in what they keep: AM keeps the carrier and both sidebands; DSB-SC both sidebands only; SSB one sideband; VSB one sideband and a vestige f<sub>v</sub> of the other.

answer.text: Bandwidth for a message of bandwidth W:
Power for a test tone with a 10 kW carrier level, from P<sub>t</sub> = P<sub>c</sub>(1 + m²/2), P<sub>DSB</sub> = P<sub>c</sub>m²/2 and P<sub>SSB</sub> = P<sub>c</sub>m²/4:

answer: At m = 1 SSB needs one sixth of the AM power; at the more typical m = 0.3 the AM transmitter spends 10.45 kW to put 0.45 kW into the sidebands (4.3 %). For the same received sideband power, the suppressed-carrier schemes save almost all the transmitter power, and SSB saves half the band as well.

Transmitter complexity: AM can be generated at high level, with an efficient class C final and a collector modulator. DSB-SC needs a balanced modulator and linear amplifiers. SSB needs a sharp sideband filter (or a phase-shift or Weaver network) and linear amplifiers. VSB needs a carefully shaped filter that is 0.5 at f<sub>c</sub>.

Receiver complexity: AM with m ≤ 1 uses a diode envelope detector, the cheapest receiver possible. DSB-SC needs coherent detection with carrier recovery (pilot, squaring loop or Costas loop). SSB needs a stable local oscillator; a frequency error shifts the voice pitch, which is tolerable for speech at a few hertz. VSB needs coherent detection, unless a large carrier is added so that an envelope detector can be used, as in analog TV.

answer.text: Summary:

head: AM
DSB-SC
SSB
VSB
rows: Power for one tone at m = 1

answer: Medium-wave broadcasting: AM. Millions of listeners need the cheapest possible receiver; one transmitter can afford the carrier power, and the 9 kHz channels fit 2W for 4.5 kHz audio.

HF point-to-point voice: SSB. Power is limited (often a battery or a small generator), the HF band is crowded, and both ends have proper receivers with stable oscillators. SSB gives the most signal per watt and per hertz.

Television video: VSB. Video has energy down to near 0 Hz, so SSB cannot be filtered; DSB would double a 5 MHz band. VSB adds only 0.75 MHz to the 5 MHz video and, with the carrier sent, still allows an envelope detector in the TV set.
Closing check: at m = 1, AM 15 kW = 10 + 2.5 + 2.5 kW, DSB-SC 5 kW = 2 × 2.5 kW and SSB 2.5 kW, so the table is consistent line by line.

bank.q: A receiver must demodulate (i) AM with m = 0.5, (ii) AM with m = 1.2, (iii) DSB-SC and (iv) SSB. Analyse whether an envelope detector or a coherent detector works for each, and work out the effect of a 30° phase error and of a 10 Hz frequency error in the local carrier for DSB-SC and SSB carrying a 1 kHz tone.
outline: DSB-SC envelope |m(t)|; SSB envelope constant for a tone
Coherent output (A<sub>c</sub>/2)m cos φ for DSB-SC
SSB: phase error shifts phase; frequency error shifts tones
DSB-SC: frequency error gives a beat
answer: An envelope detector outputs the magnitude of the envelope. It returns the message only if the envelope is A<sub>c</sub>[1 + m(t)] with 1 + m(t) ≥ 0 at all times. A coherent detector multiplies by a local cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + φ) and low-pass filters, so it returns the in-phase component, sign included.

answer.text: Case by case, with A<sub>c</sub> = 10 V and a tone:

head: Signal
Envelope
Envelope detector
Coherent detector (φ = 0)
rows: works: 2.5 cos ω<sub>m</sub>t V after DC block
|10[1 + 1.2 cos ω<sub>m</sub>t]|, folds at the troughs
gives a rectified tone at twice f<sub>m</sub>

answer: So only AM with m ≤ 1 can use the envelope detector. The coherent detector handles all four because it does not take a magnitude; for AM the DC term (A<sub>c</sub>/2) is removed afterwards.

answer.text: DSB-SC, phase error 30°: y(t) = (A<sub>c</sub>/2)m(t) cos φ.
answer.pre:
φ = 0:   y = 5 cos ω<sub>m</sub>t V
φ = 30°: y = 5 × 0.866 cos ω<sub>m</sub>t = 4.33 cos ω<sub>m</sub>t V   (13.4 % amplitude loss)
φ = 90°: y = 0   (quadrature null)

answer: DSB-SC, frequency error 10 Hz: y(t) = (A<sub>c</sub>/2) cos 2π1000t · cos 2π10t = (A<sub>c</sub>/4)[cos 2π990t + cos 2π1010t]. The listener hears a 1 kHz tone that rises and falls in loudness, reaching zero 20 times a second: unusable without carrier lock.

answer.text: SSB (USB of a 1 kHz tone on f<sub>c</sub>): the received line is cos 2π(f<sub>c</sub> + 1000)t. Multiplying by cos(2π(f<sub>c</sub> + Δf)t + φ) and low-pass filtering gives:
answer.pre:
y(t) = ½ cos(2π(1000 − Δf)t − φ)
φ = 30°, Δf = 0:  ½ cos(2π1000t − 30°)   same amplitude, phase moved
φ = 0, Δf = 10:   ½ cos 2π990t          tone shifted to 990 Hz

answer: For SSB the phase error only shifts the phase of each tone, which the ear does not notice in speech, and the amplitude is unchanged. The frequency error shifts every tone by 10 Hz (down for the USB with a high LO, up for the LSB). Speech stays intelligible for errors of a few tens of hertz but sounds unnatural; music would be ruined because the harmonic relations break.

answer.text: Summary of the effects:

answer: Closing check: for DSB-SC, the two beat components of 2.50 V each add to the full 5 V peak when cos 2π10t = 1, matching the zero-error output; and for SSB the output amplitude ½ is the same for every φ.

bank.q: A 50 kW medium-wave station uses a class C final of efficiency 80 % with collector modulation from a class B modulator of efficiency 70 %. Analyse the power flow at m = 1 and at the average programme level m = 0.3, and compare with a low-level design whose linear final has an average efficiency of 50 %. Which design should the station use, and why?
outline: P<sub>audio</sub> = P<sub>dc</sub> m²/2; modulator input P<sub>audio</sub>/η<sub>B</sub>
answer: In high-level modulation the class C final converts DC to RF at efficiency η whether the supply is steady or varied, so the carrier comes from the DC supply and the sideband power comes from the audio modulator through the modulation transformer.

answer.text: Formulas:
answer.pre:
P<sub>dc</sub>    = P<sub>c</sub>/η                      (DC input of the final)
P<sub>audio</sub> = P<sub>dc</sub> m²/2                   (audio power the modulator supplies)
P<sub>t</sub>     = P<sub>c</sub>(1 + m²/2) = η(P<sub>dc</sub> + P<sub>audio</sub>)
P<sub>mod</sub>   = P<sub>audio</sub>/η<sub>B</sub>                 (modulator's own DC input)

answer.text: High-level, P<sub>c</sub> = 50 kW, η = 0.80, η<sub>B</sub> = 0.70:
Low-level design, same output, linear final at 50 % average efficiency (the low-power modulator stage is negligible):

answer: At the average level m = 0.3 the high-level station draws 66.5 kW for 52.25 kW radiated; the low-level one draws 104.5 kW, about 38 kW more, all of it heat. Over a broadcast day of 18 hours that is about 684 kWh of extra electricity every day.

The cost of the high-level design is the audio modulator: it must deliver 31.25 kW of audio at full modulation, through a large modulation transformer that carries the final stage's DC. The low-level design avoids this but needs every RF stage after the modulator to be linear, which is what makes it inefficient.

Recommendation: high-level collector modulation (or its modern solid-state form, pulse-step modulation) for this 50 kW AM station, because a broadcast transmitter runs all day and efficiency dominates its running cost, and AM's steady carrier lets the final be class C. Low-level designs suit SSB, VSB and small transmitters, where linearity is unavoidable or the power is small.
Closing check: at m = 0.3, P<sub>t</sub> = 0.8 × (62.50 + 2.8125) = 52.25 kW, which equals P<sub>c</sub>(1 + 0.045) = 52.25 kW.

glossary.def: Modulation in which the carrier's amplitude follows the message, with the carrier itself transmitted.
m = A<sub>m</sub>/A<sub>c</sub>, the depth of amplitude modulation; m > 1 is overmodulation.
The curve joining the peaks of a modulated carrier; A<sub>c</sub>[1 + m cos 2πf<sub>m</sub>t] for tone AM.
The band of frequencies above (USB) or below (LSB) the carrier that carries the message.
The fraction of AM power in the sidebands, m²/(2 + m²).
Double-sideband suppressed-carrier modulation: both sidebands, no carrier.
Demodulation by multiplying with a local carrier of the same frequency and phase, then low-pass filtering.
Zero output of a coherent detector whose local carrier is 90° out of phase.
A carrier-recovery loop with in-phase and quadrature arms that locks a VCO to a suppressed carrier.
Single-sideband modulation: one sideband only, bandwidth W.
A filter that delays every positive-frequency component by 90°; used in the phase-shift SSB method.
Vestigial-sideband modulation: one sideband plus a small part (the vestige) of the other.
A modulator that uses the v² term of a nonlinear device to form the product of carrier and message.
Two matched nonlinear devices in push-pull whose difference output cancels the carrier, giving DSB-SC.
Four diodes in a ring switched by the carrier; a balanced modulator and mixer.
A diode with an RC load that follows the peaks of an AM wave.
Envelope-detector distortion when RC is too long to follow a falling envelope.
Flattening of the audio troughs when m exceeds R<sub>ac</sub>/R<sub>dc</sub> of the detector load.
High-level AM in which the audio varies the supply voltage of a class C final stage.
A receiver that converts every station to a fixed intermediate frequency before amplification and detection.
The fixed frequency of a superhet's IF stages, 455 kHz in AM broadcast sets.
The second input that mixes to the IF: f<sub>s</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub> with high-side injection.
Keeping the LO exactly f<sub>IF</sub> above the RF tuning across the band.
Feedback from the detector's DC level that lowers RF and IF gain on strong signals.
Frequency division multiplexing: messages share a channel in separate frequency bands.
An unused strip between FDM channels that lets real filters separate them.
